metadata.title: CRM: A Cash Gusher At A Marked-Down Price

content.text:
Salesforce is currently trading at a lower valuation multiple compared to historical averages, prompting investor debate over its intrinsic value.
Salesforce (CRM) generates free cash equal to 8.8% of its market value each year, while the median S&P 500 company manages just 4.3%. Yet over the last twelve months, as the index climbed 21%, Salesforce stock fell 17.5%. The market is making a very specific offer on this application software business, which currently trades around $190.97 a share. The question for investors is whether this is a genuine bargain on a cash machine, or a fair warning about what comes next.
Is This 8.8% Yield Built On A Durable Machine?
The cash flow is not a one-time event. It is the output of a $42.83 billion revenue business with durable profitability. Salesforce's operating margin over the last twelve months was 22%, comfortably above its 3-year average of 20%. This financial strength is rooted in its position as what management calls the "number 1 agentic CRM," selling software that automates sales, service, and marketing functions for its customers.
The company is leaning heavily into artificial intelligence to drive the next phase of growth. Its Agentforce products now represent an annual recurring revenue stream greater than $1 billion. Usage metrics are expanding rapidly; the company reported it processed 28.6 trillion tokens in its latest quarter, up 152% from the quarter prior. This is the engine: selling more AI-infused, high-margin software to a large existing customer base.
The Market Sees Lagging Bookings And A Drag From Older Clouds
For the stock's markdown to be correct, the market must believe this cash stream is set to shrink or stall. The concern, visible in the latest earnings call, is that the impressive AI adoption is not yet translating into broad-based financial strength. The investor debate centers on whether the new AI products can overcome softness in other parts of the business, such as its Tableau and Commerce Cloud offerings.
Skeptics point out that key leading indicators, like contract bookings, have not meaningfully outperformed guidance for the last 2 quarters. This raises a fair question about timing. A recent analysis asked if CRM stock passed the value-trap test, which is precisely the issue the market is weighing: are the strong AI signals enough to re-accelerate the entire company? For investors who prefer to own the entire software theme rather than a single name, a software ETF like IGV offers broader exposure.
